summary: As a 3-person tax office owner the WISP is a real legal duty, but I already meet it with a free IRS template or a one-off $699 WISP, and $297-697/yr cyber insurance gives me breach response and pre-breach legal help. Under 5,000 consumers the written IR plan isn't even required. $1,180 for year one buys too little I can't get cheaper.

objections.objection: The money has to come from the same small pot as cyber insurance, and insurance wins. Tax-preparer cyber plans cost $297-697 a year and include data breach response, pre-breach legal access, breach preparedness and staff training videos, plus real coverage. Faced with $1,180 for Safeguards Desk, I keep the policy and drop this. The incident clock and 2 support hours duplicate what my insurer's breach coach and panel counsel already do, and they pay the bills.

The must-have part is cheap; the recurring part is optional for most targets. Under 16 CFR 314.6, a firm with customer information on fewer than 5,000 consumers is exempt from 314.4(h) (written incident response plan), (d)(2) (continuous monitoring or annual pen test/vulnerability scans) and (i) (annual report to the board). That covers most 1-10 person tax offices. The tabletop and tested IR plan sold as compliance are therefore good practice, not a legal duty. I can't use the regulation to justify a subscription to myself or my accountant.

The PTIN renewal and Form W-12 wedge is weaker than the concept assumes. The W-12 question asks whether the preparer is aware of the WISP duty; it does not ask for proof of a plan. Owners already tick it holding a free Pub 5708 template. The template satisfies the trigger moment, so nothing at renewal pushes me to pay.

There is no enforcement or audit finding I can show my CFO (my spouse or my own accountant). I found no FTC Safeguards action against a small tax practice; the known tax-prep case is TaxSlayer, a large online provider, and the concept itself lists enforcement against tiny firms as an open question. The 30-day FTC clock needs 500+ affected consumers and unencrypted data, so for many offices it is a rare, once-a-decade event. Without a fear trigger this is a nice-to-have bought only after an incident.

Managed IT and hosting vendors for tax firms already sell a WISP bundled with security support the owner may already buy (ACE: flat $699 custom WISP with risk assessment and 24x7 managed security support). For offices with any IT or hosting provider, this is a second invoice for something the incumbent vendor can claim to cover.

The value to me is mostly the founder's time (onboarding, tabletop, M365 checks), not the software. If I pay for that, I'd rather pay a one-off hardening visit than an ongoing $49/month whose renewal value I can't see in a year with no incident. Churn after year one looks likely.

strongest_point: The WISP duty is real federal law owners are reminded of every year, and a hands-on Windows/M365 practitioner who tailors it beats a template a busy owner never tested.
what_would_change_my_mind: A cyber insurer or tax-preparer insurance program (e.g. the PTIN.org/NAEA plans) agrees to refer, bundle or discount premiums for firms on the program, so it replaces rather than adds to the insurance spend.
At least 3 of 10 interviewed owners show a concrete pressure: an insurer questionnaire, an IRS/FTC inquiry, a client or bank asking for proof of a tested plan, or a past incident they mishandled.
Evidence of FTC or IRS (e-file provider sanctions) enforcement reaching sub-20-person tax or mortgage offices since May 2024.

Repositioning to firms above 5,000 consumers (where 314.4(h), (d)(2) and (i) apply) or to small RIAs under Reg S-P, where the recurring IR and testing work is a legal requirement, with 3 signed annual agreements at the stated price.
First-year renewal data: at least 70% of pilot clients renew without an incident having occurred.
